sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Some Dominion sets, in addition to cards and game components printed as cards, provide other materials.

Player-specific materials are often distributed in six different colors, one for each possible player: red, blue, orange, green, white and yellow.

sections.heading: Player mats
sections.body: **Player mats** (**playmats** or **mats** for short) are pieces of cardboard used by certain cards to set aside resources for future use. {card:Island} sets aside cards on a mat until the end of the game. *{card:Pirate Ship}* and *{card:Trade Route}* set aside Tokens on a mat to keep track of {cost:} they generate when played. {card:Native Village} sets cards aside to be drawn later. Cards that produce {vp:} tokens put them on a mat to be scored at the end of the game. The **Tavern mat** is a place to keep your Reserve cards until you call them. The Coffers / Villagers mats keep coin tokens in reserve for extra {coin:+} and **+Actions** when needed. The **Trash mat** is the place to keep cards that are trashed during the game. The Exile mat is for keeping Exiled cards until they can be discarded. The Favors mat is for keeping gained Favor tokens, until they can be spent for various Allies activities.

sections.heading: Base Cards mat
sections.body: The **Dominion Base Cards Mat** is a full-color cardboard game board that was included in the Dominion Big Box, released in 2010. It has pre-printed spaces for all the base cards included in the Big Box, including {card:Estate}, {card:Duchy}, {card:Province}, {card:Colony}, {card:Curse}, {card:Copper}, {card:Silver}, {card:Gold}, {card:Platinum}, and {card:Potion}. It also has a place for the Trash pile, although the word "Trash" no longer appears on the card's art. The art chosen for all eleven of these cards is from the original version of Dominion and not from the Base Cards set. The mat has nothing else included on it and leaves no room for any Kingdom cards or future base cards, such as Ruins.

sections.heading: Tokens
sections.body: A **token** is a metal, cardboard, or wooden piece used in Dominion. They are used to track various game states that are not represented directly by cards. Some sets use tokens as one of their primary themes; some tokens are only used by a single card.

sections.heading: Victory tokens
sections.body: Victory tokens (or VP tokens, denoted by the symbol {vp:}) are metal tokens featured in Prosperity and Empires. They are metal or cardboard chips that represent victory points players earn in addition to the values of the Victory cards they possess, and are therefore an example of alt-VP. VP tokens may be earned by playing certain cards, buying certain Events, or meeting the conditions of certain Landmarks. VP tokens cannot run out; players should use a substitute if needed.

sections.heading: Coin tokens
sections.body: Coin tokens are metal tokens used in Cornucopia & Guilds, Renaissance, Allies, and the first editions of Seaside and Prosperity. Their main function is to track the game mechanics of Coffers, Villagers and Favors; in games using one of these mechanics, each player receives a mat on which they put Coin tokens to track the number of Coffers, Villagers, or Favors they have accumulated. Coin tokens are also used by *{card:Pirate Ship}*, *{card:Trade Route}*, {card:Sinister Plot}, and {card:Garrison} to track their own effects. Coin tokens cannot run out; players should use a substitute if needed.

sections.heading: Embargo tokens
sections.body: Embargo tokens were metal tokens included with first edition of Seaside. One of these tokens is placed on a Supply pile each time an *{card:Embargo}* is played, to track the number of {card:Curse|Curses} a player gains when buying a card from that pile. Embargo tokens cannot run out; players should use a substitute if needed.

sections.heading: Adventures tokens
sections.body:
Adventures comes with 10 different cardboard tokens, in each of 6 player colors. Some provide a vanilla bonus for cards from the Action card Supply piles they're on, others act as penalties, and the rest have various effects. They are used by several cards and Events.

sections.heading: Debt tokens
sections.body: Debt tokens (denoted by the symbol {debt:}) are metal tokens featured in Empires and Rising Sun (some localized Empires editions have cardboard Debt tokens, instead of metal ones). When a player possesses {debt:}, they are not permitted to buy cards (or Events or Projects). Some cards and landscapes have abilities that cause a player to accumulate {debt:} when used; other cards and Events have {debt:} in their cost, which causes players to acquire {debt:} when buying them. {debt:} cannot run out; players should use a substitute if needed.

sections.heading: Wooden cubes
sections.body: Renaissance comes with 12 wooden cubes, 2 in each of 6 player colors (1 cm on a side). Players use these to track which Projects they have purchased, and are receiving the effects of. Each player only has 2 of these cubes, which do run out.

sections.heading: Sun tokens
sections.body: Rising Sun comes with 13 wooden tokens in the form of sun icons, that are to be placed on a Prophecy card when Omen cards are used in a game. The number of tokens put on a Prophecy depends on the number of players, and is as follows: 2 players - 5 tokens, 3 players - 8 tokens, 4 players - 10 tokens, 5 players - 12 tokens, and 6 players - 13 tokens.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A **reshuffle** is when a player turns over their discard pile and shuffles it to replace their empty deck. The player has a limited amount of control over when that happens, and effectively exploiting that control to is an important element of tactical play.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
* If you have to do anything with your deck - for example draw, look at, reveal, set aside, discard, or trash cards - and you need more cards than are left in your deck, first shuffle your discard pile and put it under your deck, then do the thing.
* If there are still not enough cards, you do the thing with however many cards you can.
* If when shuffling there are no cards in your deck, the shuffled discard pile simply becomes your new deck.

* When your deck is empty, you do not shuffle until you need to do something with cards from your deck.
* If you have to put a card on top of your deck when it is empty, that card becomes the only card in your deck.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* For cases where you don't know how many cards you are accessing (e.g. {card:Library}), you are doing them one at a time, and don't shuffle until you have no cards left in your deck and need to access another one.
* The -1 card token applies as the first step of "draw N cards." This means you count it as if it were a card when determining when to reshuffle before drawing cards. This only applies to drawing cards, not other methods of accessing them.
* When shuffling {card:Stash} cards in your discard pile, you may only place those Stash cards anywhere among the shuffled cards; they cannot be placed on top of or in between any remaining cards in your deck. Also, you may look at any remaining cards in your deck before choosing where to place the Stash cards in your shuffled discard pile.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.body:
# You play a {card:Smithy} and need to draw 3 cards. However, you only have 2 cards in your (draw) Deck (and some other cards in your discard pile). In this case, you would reshuffle your discard pile, put it face down *under* the 2 cards in your deck, then you would pick up the 3 cards cards you need from your new deck (the 2 old cards and the top of the shuffled cards). You would *not* draw 2 cards first and then reshuffle and then take the top card of the new deck (though this makes no practical difference except with {card:Stash}).
# {card:Witch} is in the kingdom and your opponent has bought one. After your turn, you have 5 cards in hand and none in your draw deck, and several miscellaneous cards in your discard pile. One of the cards you have in hand is a Smithy. However, you *cannot* choose to reshuffle until your turn when you play Smithy and are required to draw cards.

In this (second) example, the timing of the reshuffle has real, practical consequences. If your opponent plays Witch (barring other conditions), you will gain a {card:Curse} to your discard pile; if your discard has already been reshuffled (when it shouldn't have been) into your new deck, you won't have the chance of drawing this Curse from Smithy. That's a distinct advantage to you.

sections.heading: Cards that make you shuffle
sections.body:
* {card:Annex} — Shuffle all but up to 5 cards from your discard pile into your deck.
* {card:Donate} — Shuffle all cards you didn't trash into your deck.
* {card:Famine} — Discard any Actions from the top three cards of your deck, then shuffle your remaining deck.
* {card:Inn} — When gained, you may shuffle any number of Action cards from your discard into your deck.

sections.heading: Cards that do something when you shuffle
sections.body:
* {card:Avoid} — The next time you shuffle this turn, pick up to 3 of those cards to put into your discard pile.
* {card:Emissary} — If the cards drawn by Emissary made you shuffle, +1 Action and +2 Favors.
* {card:Fated} — When shuffling, look through the cards and reveal any Fated cards to put them at the top or bottom.
* {card:Order of Astrologers} — When shuffling, pick one card per spent Favor to put on top.
* {card:Order of Masons} — When shuffling, pick two card per spent Favor to put into your discard.
* {card:Star Chart} — When shuffling, pick one card to put on top.
* {card:Stash} — When shuffling at least one Stash, look through your remaining deck and put the Stashes anywhere in the shuffled cards.
* All Shadows — When shuffling any Shadow cards, put all Shadow cards (in any order) below the shuffled cards.

sections.heading: Prior official rules (amended by Dominion, second edition)
sections.body:
* When his Deck is exhausted **and** the player needs to draw or reveal cards from his Deck, he shuffles his Discard pile to reform his Deck. He does not shuffle his Discard pile until he needs to reveal or draw a card from his Deck and cannot.
* At any point in the game, if a player has to draw or reveal more cards than are remaining in his Deck, he must draw or reveal as many as he can and then shuffle his face-up Discard pile to form a new face-down Deck. Then, he draws or reveals the remaining number of cards from his newly shuffled Deck.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
The default **time in Dominion at which a card has an effect** is when it is played. If an Action, Treasure, or Night card's text doesn't state specifically when the instructions on it are to be carried out, it is when the card is played. Since cards are played one at a time in Dominion (even Treasure cards), there is never any ambiguity about what order to resolve these effects in: play one card, resolving its effects; then play the next card, resolving its effects. Similarly, Events by default are resolved when you buy them.

Many cards and landscapes, however, have effects at specifically-stated other times. This page is an index of the various situations that can cause a card's abilities to be triggered. This can be interpreted as data for a flow chart: For example, if you are buying a card, look at the list of "when you buy a card" triggers to see if any of those effects apply, and if they do, execute them; then you can see if any of the effects triggered by buying a card themselves trigger other effects, and so on. It is often the case that a single trigger can activate multiple cards' abilities simultaneously, and then the abilities must be resolved one at a time using the rules below.

Some effects that take place at times other than when a card is played are thought of as being "set up" by playing a card; even though the effect itself takes place later, the act of playing the card is what causes it to happen. For example, playing the same card twice will cause the later effect to take place twice, and moving the card out of play will not prevent the set-up effect from taking place. Other effects are caused by a card being in a particular location, such as the play area, regardless of how or why it got there.

Cards in italics have been removed.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
* If multiple cards resolve at the same time on your turn (for example, Duration cards that do something “at the start of your next turn”), you choose what order to resolve them.
* A card that affects multiple players during your turn still resolves in player order, affecting you first if it affects all players and then proceeding clockwise.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* If an effect causes you to gain or draw multiple cards, you always in principle gain or draw them one at a time, resolving any on-gain or on-draw abilities of one before moving on to the next. However, if you are instructed to trash or discard multiple cards, unless that effect is explicitly sequential, they are trashed or discarded at the same time. For example, {card:Steward} can trash 2 cards; if you choose that option, you may not trash one card, resolve an on-trash effect (such as {card:Market Square}'s), then trash the other card. Both cards must be trashed simultaneously, and on-trash effects resolved with afterwards. Conversely, {card:Remake} trashes two cards, but it instructs you specifically to trash them one at a time.

* At the end of the game, your discard pile, your hand, cards you have in play, cards you've set aside, and cards you've put on mats all count as part of your deck.

sections.heading: Punctual effects
sections.body: These are abilities that are executed at a single point in time: you fully resolve the card's ability by following the instructions on the card in order, and then move on to the next ability to be resolved.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.body:
Setup instructions normally only happen once at the start of the game. They do not happen in any particular order, and should all be completely resolved before players shuffle their starting decks.

See the Setup page for all instructions related to setting up a game and a list of cards that have special instructions during setup.

:*See also: stop moving rule*

The **lose track rule** was a superseded rule covering what to do with a card when it is not where an effect expects it to be. In such situations, according to the rule, the effect is unable to move the card. This rule was officially codified in Dark Ages, though Donald X. had invoked it in card rulings previously. It was replaced by the stop moving rule.

It is possible for a card to lose track of itself, if it has an effect that tries to move itself, which is then thwarted by another effect moving it first. For example, {card:Hermit} loses track of itself when you don't buy anything in a turn, and try to trash it and gain a {card:Madman}, but use {card:Scheme} to top-deck Hermit before you trash it. Because Hermit is not in the discard pile, where it expects itself to be, it loses track of itself, and does not trash itself.

This rule only pertains to card *movement*. Other effects related to the lost card still happen, as long as they are not contingent on the movement that was prevented. For example, while Scheme prevents Hermit from moving to the trash, a Madman is still gained, since the gaining of a Madman did not depend on Hermit moving into the trash. However, a Scheme that top-decks a Traveller *will* prevent an exchange from happening, since gaining the next card in the Traveller line is contingent on the previous Traveller returning to its pile.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
* In rare circumstances an effect may try to move a card that is not where that effect expects the card to be. In those cases the card does not move - the effect has "lost track" of the card.
* Losing track of a card prevents it from being moved, but does not stop anything else from happening.
** For example, if you {card:Procession} a {card:Madman}, Procession first puts Madman in play; then you resolve Madman, getting +2 Actions and drawing cards and returning Madman to the Madman pile; then Procession fails to put Madman into play again, because Procession expects to find Madman in play, but it is not there, it's in the Madman pile; then you resolve Madman again, only getting +2 Actions this time, since it says "if you do" before the card-drawing, and you did not actually return it to the Madman pile this time; then Procession fails to trash Madman since Procession again expects to find Madman in play and it is not there; and then you gain an Action costing {cost:1} if you can.
* Cards do not lose track of cards that they move, only cards that other cards move.
** For example when Procession puts Madman into play, that does not cause Procession to lose track of Madman; it is Madman moving itself that causes Procession to lose track of it.
* Things lose track of a card if something moves it, if it is the top card of a deck and gets covered up, or if it is the top card of a discard pile and gets covered up.

Overview
sections.body: **Adventures** is the ninth expansion to Dominion, released April 2015. It is a large expansion, with 400 cards, including 30 sets of new Kingdom cards. It adds more of the popular Duration cards, and introduces Events, as well as Reserve and Traveller cards, and a variety of tokens used to track the effects of various card and Event abilities.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A **turn** is the period of time during which a player may play and buy cards, and then clean-up for their next turn. Almost all gameplay happens during a turn. Players alternate taking turns until the game ends. If a previous game has been played, the player with the fewest points of that game takes the first turn in the next one; otherwise, the first player should be determined randomly.

sections.heading: Turn phases
sections.body:
At the start of their turn, a player is given 1 Action and 1 Buy. A player may accumulate more of these as their turn progresses.
* Action phase (A) — The current player may play Action cards as long as they have Action plays remaining. The start of turn is considered to be part of the Action phase, but Action cards cannot be played normally until start-of-turn effects are finished resolving.
* Buy phase (B) — The current player may play any number of Treasure cards from their hand, and then may buy cards, Events, or Projects as long as they have Buys remaining, and enough resources remaining to buy them.
* Night phase (N) — The current player may play any number of Night cards from their hand. This phase only happens in games using Night cards.
* Clean-up phase (C) — The current player discards all cards in their hand, and all cards in play other than Duration cards (and associated Throne Room variants) that have not yet finished tracking effects are discarded. Other players also discard any cards from play that have no further effect (e.g. non-Duration cards that were played out of turn due to Reactions). Then the current player draws 5 new cards from their deck, and ends their turn.

Some cards and Events have effects that can alter the sequence of phases, for example {card:Villa} and {card:Launch}.

sections.heading: Turn count
sections.body:
It is useful to keep track of how many turns have been played by each player, for a number of reasons:
* If more than one player has the highest score at the end of the game, the player who took the fewest turns wins. If they took the same number of turns, the game remains a tie. This is partly to remedy first player turn advantage.
* In strategic discussions, the effectiveness of a strategy is often determined by the average number of turns it takes for it to gain four {card:Province|Provinces}. A pure Big Money strategy typically does this in 16 turns; adding one or two copies of certain Action cards, such as {card:Smithy} or {card:Jack of All Trades}, can drop this to anywhere from 14 to 11 turns. This metric is less useful in engine or slog mirrors; the former is more concerned with gaining all (or most) of the Provinces in one or two turns after building up their deck, while the latter is slowed down by powerful Attacks.

sections.heading: Turn order
sections.body: Whenever an effect happens to more than one player, or multiple effects involving different players try to resolve at the same time, they are resolved in turn order, starting with the player whose turn it is (or the player who last took a turn). This is important particularly with regards to gaining cards: for example, if a player plays {card:Witch}, and there's only one {card:Curse} left, only the player next in turn order gains a Curse.

sections.heading: Extra turns
sections.body:
Three cards ({card:Outpost}, {card:Possession} and {card:Voyage}) and five additional card-shaped things ({card:Fleet}, {card:Island Folk}, {card:Journey}, {card:Mission}, and {card:Seize the Day}) allow a player to take more turns than normal, each with its own penalties or restrictions. These extra turns do not add to a player's turn count, and are not used in breaking ties.

Extra turns happen in turn order — if a player plays Outpost and Possession on their turn, the Outpost turn happens first. The Possession turn is not their turn, but the turn of the next player; they are simply controlling what happens.

In 2023, Donald X. introduced errata to prevent players from getting more than one extra turn at a time in most cases.

sections.heading: Skip turns
sections.body:
One card, {card:Lich}, can cause you to skip turns. Skipping a turn means that the next time you would take a turn, you don't; nothing happens for that turn: no "start of turn" abilities, no phases. Play continues with the player to your left as usual.
* You can skip an extra turn, like one from {card:Voyage}.
* Skipped turns still count for the tiebreaker however they would have if taken.
* Abilities that refer to your "last turn" or "next turn" skip the skipped turn as well. If you play a {card:Caravan} and skip a turn, the Caravan will draw you a card on the next turn you actually take; if someone plays a {card:Smugglers} they'll gain a copy of a card you gained on the last turn you actually had.

sections.heading: Between turns
sections.body:
A few decisions, usually deciding which of multiple extra turns should occur first, take place between turns. In those cases, the player who took the last turn is considered to be in control, and is the one who makes such decisions. It does not matter if that player was Possessed on the previous turn; it is still their decision.

The original versions of {card:Donate} and {card:Mountain Pass}, from Empires, resolve between turns (so that {card:Possession} is not in effect when decisions are made), but revisions of these cards have those abilities take place during the turn.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
**Dominion: Cornucopia & Guilds** is a box that contains the 5th expansion Cornucopia and the 8th expansion Guilds, which are no longer printed separately. First, it came with a special {card:Bane|Bane card} to act as a marker for {card:Young Witch}. Second, it included 6 {card:Coffers mats} for use with certain cards that mention Coffers. And third, it included a new combined rulebook for both expansions, which also reflects changes made to the rules in the revised edition of the game.

The Second Edition of this box received new box art, replaced eight Kingdom cards and the Prizes from the first edition, and includes updated {card:Coffers mats}.

sections.heading: Overpay
sections.body:
Some cards can be "overpaid" for. The costs for these cards have a "+" next to the coin symbol. A player may pay any additional amount for such a card, and then gets an effect based on how much extra was paid.
* {card:Potion|Potions} (from Dominion: Alchemy) may be used in overpaid amounts if desired, although this is only meaningful with {card:Stonemason}.
* Debt (from Dominion: Empires) cannot be overpaid.
* Players may choose not to overpay, even if they have extra coins, but cannot choose to overpay {cost:0}; to overpay, a player has to actually pay more than the cost.
* Players can only overpay for a card when buying it, not when gaining it some other way.
* Overpaying itself happens when a card is bought; however "overpay" abilities happen when the card is gained, and are timed with other such abilities.
* The "+" is just a reminder; a card with a "+" in its cost still has its normal cost for all purposes. For example, {card:Infirmary} costs {cost:3}, so it can be the card set aside for Ferryman.
* Reducing the costs of cards via cards like {card:Renown} does not make overpaying cheaper; for example if you had {cost:5} and two Renowns in play and bought {card:Farrier}, Farrier would cost {cost:0}, and overpaying with your {cost:5} would still only give you +5 Cards at end of turn.

The **"no visiting" rule** is a rule dictating that when a card is gained to a place other than the discard pile (such as to the top of a player's deck), that card does not "visit" the discard pile; in other words, the card is not put into the discard pile before going to its final destination, but goes directly to where it is being gained to. This is important when used in conjunction with the stop moving rule; cards that are gained to a location other than the discard pile can be moved away from their gain location by an effect looking for a gained card.

However, in other cases a card might not be gained directly to a place other than the discard pile, but rather gained to the discard pile and then subsequently moved. In these cases the stop moving rule can interfere.

Example 1: If you {card:Summon} a {card:Nomad Camp}, even though the Nomad Camp is not in the discard pile (because it was gained directly to the top of your deck), Summon will still be able to set it aside. In contrast, if you Summon a {card:Nomads}, and then use {card:Travelling Fair} to move it onto your deck, that will cause Summon to fail to set aside the Nomads.

Example 2: If you gain a card with {card:Workshop}, and then move it onto your deck with {card:Watchtower}, that will cause {card:Gatekeeper} to fail to exile the card. In contrast, if you gain a card with {card:Armory}, it will be exiled by Gatekeeper.

sections.body: * When a card is gained to a location other than a discard pile, it does not "visit" the discard pile – it goes directly to where it was gained. For example {card:Armory} gains cards directly to the top of a deck.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: **Nocturne** is the eleventh expansion to Dominion, released in November 2017. The box contains 33 sets of Kingdom cards. It introduces Night cards, which are played after your Buy phase; Heirlooms, which replace your starting {card:Copper|Coppers}; and Fate and Doom cards, which give out Boons and Hexes, respectively.

sections.heading: Additional rules
sections.body:
* Nocturne adds Night cards and the Night phase. In games using Night cards, the Night phase happens after the Buy phase - it goes, Action, Buy, Night, Clean-up. In your Night phase, you can play any number of Night cards.

* Nocturne has cards with a yellow banner saying "Heirloom" and naming a card. In games using a card with that banner, each player replaces a starting {card:Copper} with the named card. See Preparation.

* Nocturne has Fate cards and Boons. Fate cards can somehow give players Boons; all the Fate type means is that the Boons are shuffled at the start of the game. Boons are a face-down deck of cards that are revealed as needed. The phrase "receive a Boon" means, turn over the top Boon, and follow the instructions on it. If the Boons deck is empty, first shuffle the discarded Boons to reform the deck; you may also do this any time all Boons are in their discard pile. Received Boons normally go to the Boons discard pile, but three ({card:The Field's Gift}, {card:The Forest's Gift}, and {card:The River's Gift}) go in front of a player until that turn's Clean-up.

* Nocturne also has Doom cards and Hexes. Doom cards can somehow give players Hexes; all the Doom type means is that the Hexes are shuffled at the start of the game. Hexes are a face-down deck of cards that are revealed as needed. The phrase "receive a Hex" means, turn over the top Hex, and follow the instructions on it. "Each other player receives the next Hex" means, turn over just one Hex, and the other players all follow the instructions on that same Hex. If all Hexes have been used, shuffle the discards to reform the deck; do this whenever the deck is empty. Received Hexes always go to the Hexes discard pile.

* Three Hexes and one Kingdom card give players a State; this is a card that goes in front of a player and applies a rule. {card:Deluded} and {card:Envious} affect a single turn, and then are returned; {card:Miserable} and {card:Twice Miserable} affect scoring at the end of the game; {card:Lost in the Woods} affects one player's turns until another player takes it. Deluded and Envious are on the same card; have the relevant side face-up. Similarly Miserable and Twice Miserable are on the same card. A State only applies while a player has it.

* Boons, Hexes, and States are never in a player's deck; like Events and Landmarks (from Adventures and Empires), they are physically cards but are not "cards" in game terms. They are thus never "cards in play," receiving Boons and Hexes or taking a State is not "gaining a card," and so on.

* Nocturne has Duration cards, which were introduced in Dominion: Seaside.
 (older cards and this turn's cards).

* Nocturne has three cards that tell a player to "exchange" a card for another card. The card being exchanged is returned to its Supply pile, or non-Supply pile, and the card being exchanged for is taken and put into the player's discard pile. This does not count as gaining a card. The exchange only happens if both cards can be exchanged; if the pile is empty, the cards are not exchanged.

If {card:Fool} is being used, get Lost in the Woods and have it handy. If {card:Vampire} is being used, put the {card:Bat} pile near the Supply. The **stop moving rule** is a rule covering when an effect is allowed to move a card. It supersedes the lose track rule and was introduced as part of the 2019 Errata.

As with the rule version prior to this renamed one, it only pertains to card *movement*. Other effects related to a card that has been moved elsewhere first by another effect still happen, as long as they are not contingent on the movement that was prevented. However, due to another ruling posted thereto, an effect that won't happen is playing a card, i.e. when you're told to by a card, such as with {card:Vassal} or {card:Sailor} (the exception being Throne-like cards' replay ability), and the targeted card has been lost track of.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
* An effect can move a card if it specifies where the card is coming from, or if the effect put the card where it is now.
* If a card isn't where the effect would expect it to be, or has moved away from there and then back, it can't move the card.
** Played cards expect to be in play; they can't move themselves if they aren't.
** Gained cards are expected to be where they were gained to, even if this isn't the discard pile.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
A **pile** is a stack of cards. Most cards in the game have a pile associated with them, usually in the Supply, that contains multiple copies of that card. However, a handful of piles contain multiple differently-named cards (including "split piles"), are located outside the Supply, or both. The Trash pile and players' discard piles and decks are not considered "piles" when game rules and card text refer to piles, as these card stacks do not have any association to specific cards.

Piles have their own names and types that can be different to the cards within them, although most of the time they are the same. If the pile is for a Kingdom card, the name and types of the pile match those found on its randomizer. Some effects refer to card piles instead of cards which can cause surprising outcomes when combined with split piles. For example, {card:Populate} can gain a {card:Fortune} if it is currently on top of the {card:Gladiator/Fortune} pile because the pile has an Action type according to its randomizer.

Some cards are not considered to have a pile, and so any effect that impacts a card pile or tries to return a card to its pile will fail for these cards. For example, you can safely play {card:Way of the Horse} on {card:Necropolis} without losing your Necropolis. The exchange keyword relies on being able to successfully return a card to its pile in order to work. The following cards are considered to be pileless:
* Shelters
* Heirlooms
* Zombies
* The cards set aside by {card:Riverboat} and {card:Way of the Mouse}
* Cards from the {card:Black Market} deck
* Cards from piles that have been removed by {card:Divine Wind}

Piles still exist even when they are empty, you can still return cards to them and place Adventures tokens on them. Only Divine Wind can remove a pile; removed piles are not considered to be empty and no longer count for a three-pile ending even if they were empty before being removed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Certain cards and card-shaped things have **setup instructions**. If such a card is selected for inclusion in a game of Dominion, the setup instructions must be carried out before the game begins, alongside the ordinary setup procedures of preparing the Kingdom card piles, constructing and shuffling players' starting decks, etc.

Not all modifications to setup are listed as such on the cards. A few setup procedures are listed in rulebooks and apply to multiple cards, instead of appearing on the cards themselves. For example, if a card with {potion} in its cost is in use, the {card:Potion} pile is added to the supply during setup; if any card of the Liaison type is present, an Ally is selected during setup and each player starts the game with a Favor token.

A card's setup instructions are carried out any time the card is being used in the game, regardless of whether it is present in the Kingdom or included in the game outside the Supply by some other means (such as via {card:Black Market}, {card:Way of the Mouse}, {card:Ferryman}, or {card:Riverboat}).

If the setup instructions on a card results in additional cards with setup instructions being added to the game, those instructions must also be followed. For example Ferryman choosing Black Market, which triggers the setup of a Black Market deck, which includes a Liaison, which sets up {card:Approaching Army}, which adds {card:Young Witch} to the kingdom, etc. Landscapes that select a Kingdom or Supply card as their setup (i.e. {card:Obelisk} and all Traits) must do so last to take into account all available cards that may have been added due to other setup instructions.

If {card:Divine Wind} is activated, when new cards are added to the Kingdom their setup abilities may need to be performed mid-game; however any setup done for the original Kingdom cards are not undone when they are removed from the game. When Divine Wind is activated it is too late to change players' starting decks, so setup effects involving Heirlooms do not take place.

sections.heading: Basic rules
sections.body:
* Add the basic card piles ({card:Curse}, {card:Copper}, {card:Silver}, {card:Gold}, {card:Estate}, {card:Duchy}, {card:Province}) to the Supply.
* Adjust the Curse pile to contain 10 cards per player after the first, i.e. 10 for 2 players, 20 for 3 players, etc.
* Each player gets a starting deck consisting of 7 Coppers and 3 Estates. Note that all unused Coppers go in their Supply pile while the Estate Supply pile always contain exactly 12 or 8 cards (depending on the number of players).
* Choose 10 Kingdom piles to add to the Supply.
* In a 2-player game, reduce all Victory piles (both basic and Kingdom) to 8 cards instead of 12.
* In games with more than 4 players, add 3 Provinces per additional player (i.e. 15 in total for 5 players and 18 for 6 players) and optionally add a second set of Copper, Silver, and Gold cards to their piles.

sections.heading: Additional general rules
sections.body:
* Choose whether to include {card:Platinum}, and {card:Colony} in the Supply. The suggested method is to include them if the first selected Kingdom card was from Prosperity.
* Choose whether all players should replace their starting Estates with Shelters. The suggested method is to replace them if the 10th selected Kingdom card was from Dark Ages.
* Optionally choose landscapes (Events, Landmarks, Projects, Ways, and Traits) to use in the game. The suggest method is to shuffle them with the Kingdom randomizers and use no more than 2 in total.
* For every Trait used, choose a random Action or Treasure Kingdom pile that the Trait's effect will apply to. This can include piles added by {card:Young Witch} or {card:Approaching Army}. If using multiple Traits, choose a different pile for each Trait.
* Make any additional components (non-Supply card, tokens, and mats) available that are referred to by any Kingdom card.

sections.heading: Setup for groups of cards
sections.body:
These instructions only happen once, even if multiple cards of the type are present.
* Doom cards — Prepare the Hexes deck by shuffling it.
* Fate cards — Prepare the Boons deck by shuffling it.
* Knight pile — Shuffle the Knight cards into a face-down pile and turn the top card face up.
* Liaison cards — Choose a random Ally and all players start with 1 Favor.
* Looter cards — Shuffle the Ruins, put 10 per player after the first (i.e. the same as the number of Curses in the game) into a face-down pile, turn the top card face up, and add the pile to the Supply.
* Omen cards — Choose a random Prophecy and add {sun} tokens to it based on the number of players (5 tokens with 2 players, 8 with 3, 10 with 4, 12 with 5, and 13 with 6).
* Cards with {potion} in their cost — Add the {card:Potion} pile to the Supply.
* Cards referring to Loot — Shuffle the Loot cards into a face-down pile.

sections.heading: Heirlooms
sections.body: Cards with an Heirloom banner ({card:Cemetery}, {card:Fool}, {card:Pixie}, {card:Pooka}, {card:Secret Cave}, {card:Shepherd}, {card:Tracker}) — All players replace one of their starting Coppers with the Heirloom indicated on the respective card.

sections.heading: Setup instructions printed on individual cards
sections.body: Setup abilities have a range of functions. Some apply to cards whose abilities might change over the course of the game and merely provide a means of tracking those changes. Others apply to cards whose abilities change *between games*, and indicate how the abilities for *this* game are to be selected. Finally, some setup rules actually change the initial conditions of the game, in a way that may affect even players who never interact with the card-shaped thing providing the setup instructions.

sections.heading: Tracking the card's effects during the game
sections.body:
* {card:Aqueduct} — Put {vp:8} each on the {card:Silver} and {card:Gold} piles that will be moved when cards are gained and taken when gaining Victory cards.
* {card:Arena} — Put {vp:6} per player on Arena that can be taken by discarding an Action card at the start of your Buy phase.
* {card:Basilica} — Put {vp:6} per player on Basilica that can be taken by having extra {cost:} when gaining cards in your Buy phase.
* {card:Baths} — Put {vp:6} per player on Baths that can be taken by not gaining any cards during your turn.
* {card:Battlefield} — Put {vp:6} per player on Battlefield that can be taken by gaining Victory cards.
* {card:Colonnade} — Put {vp:6} per player on Colonnade that can be taken by gaining Action cards you have copies of in play.
* {card:Defiled Shrine} — Put {vp:2} on each non-Gathering Action Supply pile that will be moved when cards are gained and taken when gaining Curses.
* {card:Labyrinth} — Put {vp:6} per player on Labyrinth that can be taken when playing multiple Action cards per turn.
* *{card:Trade Route}* — Put a coin token to each Victory Supply pile to track which piles cards have been gained from.

sections.heading: Selecting the card's ability for this game
sections.body:
* {card:Black Market} — Make a Black Market deck out of unused Kingdom cards whose cards can be bought when playing Black Market. Shuffle the deck and place it face down.
* {card:Druid} — Set aside the top three Boons as options to be received when playing Druids.
* {card:Ferryman} — Choose an unused Kingdom card pile costing {cost:3} or {cost:4} whose cards will be gained together with each gained Ferryman.
* {card:Obelisk} — Choose a random Action Supply pile whose cards will be worth {vp:2} each when scoring. This can include piles added by {card:Young Witch} and {card:Approaching Army} as well as the Ruins pile (if present).
* {card:Riverboat} — Choose an unused non-Duration Action card costing {cost:5} that will be played when playing Riverboats.
* {card:Way of the Mouse} — Choose an unused non-Duration Action card costing {cost:2} or {cost:3} that can be played by using Way of the Mouse.

sections.heading: Changing the game's starting conditions
sections.body:
* {card:Approaching Army} — Add an additional Attack Kingdom card pile to the Supply.
* {card:Baker} — All players start with 1 Coffers.
* {card:Importer} — All players start with 5 Favors instead of 1.
* {card:Inherited} — All players replace one of their starting cards with an Inherited card. This happens after adding Shelters and Heirlooms.
* {card:Necromancer} — Put the three Zombies in the trash.
* {card:Tax} — Add {debt:1} to each Supply pile.
* {card:Young Witch} — Add an additional Kingdom card pile to the Supply costing {cost:2} or {cost:3} that can be revealed to block Young Witch's attack.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
**Seaside** is the second expansion to Dominion by Donald X. Vaccarino , released in 2009 by publisher Rio Grande Games. The box originally contained 26 sets of Kingdom cards, 3 types of player mats, a set of Coin tokens, and a set of {card:Embargo} tokens. The main gameplay theme of Seaside is cards whose abilities affect future turns—whether by being Duration cards, interacting with the top of the deck, or otherwise.

**Seaside (Second Edition)** was released in June 2022. 8 first-edition Kingdom card piles (and 11 blank cards) were replaced with 9 new ones. The new cards are also available in an update pack provided to allow existing Seaside sets to be updated to the second-edition form.

sections.heading: Additional first- and second-edition rules
sections.body:
Seaside introduces Duration cards.

Examples:
* You play a {card:Fishing Village}, getting +2 Actions and {coin:+1}. Since it also does something next turn, you do not discard it from play in Clean-up. At the start of your next turn, you get +1 Action and {coin:+1}. Fishing Village is now done, but stays in play through that turn, and is discarded in Clean-up.
* At the start of your turn, you have a {card:Wharf} in play from last turn. You get +2 Cards and +1 Buy. Then this turn you play a second Wharf, getting +2 Cards and +1 Buy. In Clean-up you discard the Wharf from last turn, but not the Wharf from this turn.
* You play Throne Room on a {card:Merchant Ship}. You get {coin:+2} and another {coin:+2}, for {coin:+4} total. In Clean-up both the Throne Room and Merchant Ship stay in play. At the start of your next turn you get another {coin:+4}; in that turn's Clean-up you discard the Throne Room and Merchant Ship.
* You play {card:Tactician} with no cards left in your hand. Since Tactician only does something on the next turn if you had at least one card, Tactician has nothing left to do, so you discard it in Clean-up.

sections.body: See Recommended Kingdoms/Seaside

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
**Prosperity** is the fourth Dominion expansion, released in October 2010. The box contains 25 sets of Kingdom cards. The basic conceptual theme of the set is wealth, focusing on Treasure cards and on expensive cards with powerful abilities. It is a full size expansion, and it is best known for featuring a variety of powerful game-changing cards, including the two new basic cards, {card:Colony} and {card:Platinum}, as well as cards that produce {vp:} tokens. Prosperity also introduced the first Treasure cards that have effects in addition to simply providing {coin:+}. It was the first expansion to feature cards costing {cost:7}, and the only one to have no cards costing {cost:2}. It thereby has the highest average card cost of all expansions.

The second edition of Prosperity was released in June 2022. It contains 9 new sets of Kingdom cards, which are also available on their own as an update pack, to allow existing Prosperity sets to be updated to the second-edition form.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body:
* Prosperity includes two new base cards, {card:Platinum} and {card:Colony}. You can include them whenever you want to; they are always used together. If you want to determine when to use them randomly, choose a random Kingdom card being used, and if it is from Prosperity, use {card:Platinum} and {card:Colony}. When used, they are in the Supply and can be bought and gained, but they do not take the place of Kingdom cards; you still have the usual 10 Kingdom cards. Use 8 copies of {card:Colony} for games with 2 players, 12 for games with 3 or more players. Use all 12 {card:Platinum|Platinums} with any number of players.
* Prosperity has player mats for tracking {vp:} tokens. You do not have to use one; if you do, take one when you first have {vp:} tokens. There is also a mat for {card:Trade Route}. In games using {card:Trade Route}, put out the mat at the start of the game, and put a Coin token on each Victory card pile in the Supply.

sections.heading: Platinum and Colony
sections.body: * In games using {card:Platinum} and {card:Colony}, there is an additional way the game can end. At the end of each turn, the game ends if one of these three conditions is met: the Supply pile of {card:Province} cards is empty OR any 3 Supply piles are empty (4 piles in a 5-6 player game) OR the Supply pile of {card:Colony} cards is empty.

sections.heading: Victory tokens
sections.body:
* The {vp:} tokens are simply tokens that are worth {vp:} at the end of the game. They provide a way to score that is not cards in a player's deck.
* They come in {vp:1} and {vp:5} amounts; make change as needed. They are not counter-limited; use a replacement if you run out.
* Cards say "{vp:+1}" (or other amounts) to indicate that a player takes {vp:} tokens. Cards that give {vp:+} take the tokens from the pile of unused tokens, not from a player.
* {vp:} tokens are not private; anyone can count them.

sections.heading: Special Treasures
sections.body:
* Prosperity includes nine Treasure cards with rules on them. They are in the Supply if selected as one of the 10 Kingdom cards for the game; they are not part of the Basic Supply. They are just like normal Treasures, but have special abilities. They are played during the Buy phase like normal Treasures and are affected by cards that refer to Treasures.
* Players may play Treasure cards in any order, and may choose not to play some (or all) of the Treasure cards they have in hand. The order can matter; for example {card:Bank} counts Treasures played before it, and itself, but not Treasures played after it.
* During the Buy phase, playing Treasures comes strictly before buying cards; once a card is bought, no further Treasures can be played. This can be important, for example with {card:Grand Market} or {card:Mint}.

sections.heading: Recommended sets of 10
sections.body: See Recommended Kingdoms/Prosperity.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: **Promotional cards** are official Dominion Kingdom cards and Events which do not belong to any particular set. They are a result of Donald X. trying to meet the requests of his publishers, and typically either released to help promote Dominion at conventions (such as Origins or GenCon) or to commemorate the anniversary of another game, to help promote both. Some promo cards are developed specifically for the sake of the promotion, such as {card:Governor}; others are cards that have already been developed but for which there wasn't space in a regular expansion, such as {card:Marchland}.

sections.heading: Obtaining The Promo Cards
sections.body:
* The cards can typically be purchased on the BGG store.
* Occasionally, game stores or conventions will offer the Promotional cards in conjunction with a purchase.
* Various iterations of the Big Box have included one or more Promotional cards, {card:Black Market} was included in Special Edition, and {card:Summon} was bundled with pre-release orders of Adventures German version.
* Tournaments may offer Promo cards as prizes.

**Cost reduction** is a recurring mechanic in Dominion. Rather than directly fielding coin, **cost-reducers** decrease the cost of cards, an effect which becomes more valuable with more buys or gainers. Typical cost reduction instructions follow this wording:

:*This turn, all cards cost {cost:X} less.*

sections.heading: Cost reduction
sections.body:
* Costs cannot go below {cost:0}.
* Reducing a cost in {cost:} does not reduce a cost in {debt:} or {potion}.
* Reducing the cost of cards does not affect the cost of Events or Projects.

sections.heading: Unusual cost (official rules from Menagerie)
sections.body:
* When these cards change cost, all copies of them change everywhere, for all purposes. For example, when you {card:Remodel} one of the cards, the changed cost is what matters, not the printed cost. When another player has an effect that cares what the cost of their cards is on your turn (such as the promo {card:Governor}), they use the same changed cost that you do.
* Costs cannot go below {cost:0}.
* Destrier and Fisherman [and Peddler] are also affected by other things that change costs, like {card:Bridge} (from Intrigue).
* Costs can change in the middle of resolving effects. The key thing is to follow card instructions in order.
* Example: You buy {card:Stonemason} (from Guilds) and overpay {cost:3}. You gain a {card:Goatherd}; then, since Wayfarer now costs {cost:3}, you choose to gain a Wayfarer.
* Example: You buy {card:Border Village} (from Hinterlands), which costs {cost:6}. When you gain it, you gain a cheaper card; you choose to gain a Destrier, which costs {cost:5} due to gaining the Border Village.
* Example: You play Stonemason to trash a card. If you trash {card:Gold}, you could gain a {card:Duchy}, and then could gain a Destrier, since it would then cost {cost:5}. You could gain a Duchy and then a Wayfarer the same way. If you trash a {card:Silver} and have an empty discard pile, you could gain a Fisherman, but not a second one, as then your discard pile would have a card in it, the Fisherman you gained. If you trash a Destrier, you could first gain a Duchy, which costs less than {cost:6}; then you would have to gain a card costing up to {cost:4}, as Destrier would now cost {cost:5}.
* Example: If you use {card:Trader} (from Hinterlands) to trash a Destrier, you will gain six Silvers; first it checks the cost, then you gain that many Silvers. Similarly you could trash a Wayfarer for six Silvers, and a Fisherman for two or five Silvers depending on whether or not your discard pile was empty when you trashed the Fisherman.
* These examples all assume no other gains previously in the turn. A Stonemason trashing {card:Estate} could gain two Destriers if you gained 5 other cards first; if you gain a card costing {cost:4} and then trash a Wayfarer to Trader, you will gain 4 Silvers since it costs {cost:4} then, and so on.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* Cost-reducers are generally only in effect during your turns, which means that they have no effect on card costs during scoring. However {card:Cheap}, {card:Family of Inventors}, and {card:Flourishing Trade} are exceptions as they are not limited to turns. This matters when scoring with {card:Plateau Shepherds}.
* Cost-reducers are never in effect during setup, so for example the Bane card for {card:Young Witch} cannot be a Cheap {card:Smithy}.
** This applies in the middle of the game as well: even if you have cost reduction in effect when {card:Divine Wind} adds Young Witch to the kingdom, the cost reduction will not affect the selection of the Bsne.

sections.heading: List of cost-reducers
sections.body:
Cards in *italics* have been removed.

* {card:Bridge} — the archetypal cost-reducer
* {card:Bridge Troll} — durational cost-reducer
* {card:Canal} — reduces costs on your turns for the rest of the game
* {card:Cheap} — reduces cost of a randomly chosen Supply pile for the entire game
* {card:Family of Inventors} — reduces cost of a Supply pile of your choice, for everyone
* {card:Flourishing Trade} — permanently provides cost reduction on everything for the rest of the game
* {card:Ferry} — reduces a single Supply pile's cost by {cost:2} on your turns
* {card:Highway} — cantrip
* {card:Inventor} — gains a card costing up to {cost:4} *before* its cost reduction kicks in
* *{card:Princess}* — reduces costs by {cost:2}, but only one copy exists
* {card:Quarry} — reduces Action cards by {cost:2}
* {card:Renown} — reduces costs by {cost:2}, but only one or two copies exist

sections.heading: List of cards that can change their own cost
sections.body:
These cards have a base cost which can be changed by something that happens during your turn. Of these, three are in the Menagerie expansion
* {card:Destrier} — cost is reduced by the number of cards you gained on that same turn
* {card:Fisherman} — cost is reduced by {cost:3} if you have no cards in your discard pile
* {card:Peddler} — cost is reduced by {cost:2} per Action card in play, but only during your Buy phase
* {card:Wayfarer} — cost is equal to the cost of the last-gained card, and can even become *more* expensive than its base price
{card:Animal Fair}, also from Menagerie, is an odd case: it can be bought for {cost:0} if you trash an Action card from your hand, but its numerical cost doesn't change as part of this effect.

sections.body: **Renaissance** is the twelfth expansion to Dominion. The box contains 25 sets of Kingdom cards. It features the return of Coffers, first seen in Cornucopia & Guilds, and introduces Villagers, Projects, and Artifacts.

To **trash** is to remove a card from your deck, placing it in an area called the **Trash** or **Trash pile**. This is distinct from discarding, which removes a card from your hand or other area to your discard pile, waiting to be shuffled back into your deck. Trashing a card usually means removing it permanently from your deck, although there are a small number of trash gainers (for example, {card:Lurker}) that can retrieve cards from the trash, and a few cards, {card:Fortress}, {card:Lich}, and {card:Trail}, which can return themselves to you if you try to trash them. In addition to these, some cards like {card:Forager} and {card:Necromancer} have effects that depend on what is in the trash; and the Zombies start the game in the trash. Cards that can move cards to the trash include trashers and trashing attacks; cards that trash themselves are often called one-shots. There are also cards that give an effect when they are trashed.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
: "Trash a card" - Put a card into the Trash pile.
* This is a way of getting rid of a card; a trashed card is no longer one of your cards.
* The Trash pile is on the Trash mat, face up; players may look through the Trash at any time.
* The order of the Trash pile does not matter; players can reorder it.
* Cards in the Trash are essentially out of the game, though some expansion cards can get them.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body: * Under ordinary circumstances, when an ability allows you to trash multiple cards (e.g., {card:Steward} or {card:Chapel}), you trash them all at once, before anything else happens, including any on-trash effects that are triggered by trashing the cards. {card:Remake} and {card:Monastery} are exceptions to this: they both trash cards one at a time, triggering on-trash effects in between.

sections.heading: Trashers
sections.body:
Many cards allow cards to be trashed. These are categorized in several groups:
* Trasher is the general term for cards that allow a player to trash one of their own cards, often for deck-thinning purposes. Two important categories of trashers include:
** Remodeler — Cards that trash a card and then gain a card based on the trashed card's cost.
** Trash for benefit — Cards that trash a card and provide some other benefit based on the trashed card's cost.
* Trashing attack — Attacks that make other players trash cards.
* One-shot — Cards that trash themselves, meaning they can normally only be used once.

The Trashing token (placed with {card:Plan}) can turn any card from an Action Supply pile into an on-gain trasher.

A few abilities allow players to trash a card from the Supply, rather than one of their own cards: {card:Lurker}, {card:Salt the Earth}, and {card:Gladiator}.

sections.heading: When-trash effects
sections.body: Several cards do something either when they are trashed or when another card is trashed, without being trashers themselves. These can be found on the when-trash page.

sections.heading: Gainers
sections.body: Cards that gain from the trash can be found on the trash gainer page.

sections.heading: Caring about cards in the trash
sections.body:
The following cards care about the content of the trash without gaining them.
* {card:Forager} — Produces {coin:+1} per differently named Treasure card in the trash.
* {card:Necromancer} — Plays a non-Duration Action card in the trash, leaving it there.
* {card:Mountain Shrine} — Produces +2 Cards if there are any Action cards in the trash.

**Overpaying** is a mechanic in the Cornucopia & Guilds expansion. Some cards allow the player to spend more coins than their cost when buying them, for additional effects. Such cards have a "+" added to their cost symbol. Cards having an overpay effect are:

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
Some cards can be "overpaid" for. The costs for these cards have a "+" next to the coin symbol. A player may pay any additional amount for such a card, and then gets an effect based on how much extra was paid.
* {card:Potion|Potions} (from Dominion: Alchemy) may be used in overpaid amounts if desired, although this is only meaningful with {card:Stonemason}.
* Debt (from Dominion: Empires) cannot be overpaid.
* Players may choose not to overpay, even if they have extra coins, but cannot choose to overpay {cost:0}; to overpay, a player has to actually pay more than the cost.
* Players can only overpay for a card when buying it, not when gaining it some other way.
* Overpaying itself happens when a card is bought; however "overpay" abilities happen when the card is gained, and are timed with other such abilities.
* The "+" is just a reminder; a card with a "+" in its cost still has its normal cost for all purposes. For example, {card:Infirmary} costs {cost:3}, so it can be the card set aside for {card:Ferryman}.
* Reducing the costs of cards via cards like {card:Renown} does not make overpaying cheaper; for example if you had {cost:5} and two Renowns in play and bought {card:Farrier}, Farrier would cost {cost:0}, and overpaying with your {cost:5} would still only give you +5 Cards at end of turn.

sections.heading: Deprecated official rules (2021)
sections.body:
* Some cards can be "overpaid" for. The costs for these cards have a "+" next to the coin symbol. A player may pay any additional amount for such a card, and then gets an effect based on how much extra was paid.
* Potions (from Dominion: Alchemy) may be used in overpaid amounts if desired, although this is not always meaningful.
* Debt (from Dominion: Empires) cannot be overpaid.
* Players may choose not to overpay, even if they have extra coins, but cannot choose to overpay by {cost:0}; to overpay, a player has to actually pay more than the cost.
* The coins used to overpay are gone after spending them to overpay; they cannot be then used to buy something else.
* Overpaying happens when a card is bought, which is before it is gained.
* Players can only overpay for a card when buying it, not when gaining it some other way.
* The "+" is just a reminder; a card with "+" in the cost still has its normal cost for all purposes. For example if a player plays {card:Haggler} (from Dominion: Hinterlands), then buys a {card:Masterpiece}, overpaying, Haggler will still gain them a card costing less than {cost:3}, the cost of Masterpiece. Similarly, Masterpiece could be the Bane card for {card:Young Witch}, since it costs {cost:3}.
* Reducing the costs of cards via cards like {card:Bridge} (from Dominion: Intrigue) does not interact with overpay; for example, if you play five Bridges and have {cost:5} total to spend, Herald would cost {cost:0}, but if you bought one the most you could overpay for it would still be {cost:5}.

sections.heading: List of cards
sections.body:
Cards in *italics* have been removed.

* *{card:Doctor}* — For each {cost:1} you overpaid to look at the top card of your deck; and you can choose to trash it, discard it, or put it back.
* {card:Farrier} — Increase your handsize for the next turn by the amount you overpaid.

The Event {card:Asceticism}, from Rising Sun, has an ability similar to overpaying, though it doesn't use that term in its instructions.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
To **reveal** a card is to show it publicly for all other players to see. This can be done from your hand, your deck, or your discard pile; any area whose contents are not public knowledge. Once revealed, there is usually an instruction given for what to do with the card; if there is none, it is assumed that you put it back where it came from. Many cards reveal for different reasons; digging cards reveal cards until revealing one meeting their condition, and reactions are usually revealed when they are activated. One card, {card:Patron}, has a special effect that is triggered *when* it is revealed by some other card.

However, if a card says to *look at* another card, you explicitly *do not* show it to other players, but you similarly put it back where it came from if no other instruction is given.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
: "Reveal a card" - All players get to see the card.
* After revealing it, return it to wherever it was (unless otherwise instructed).

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body: * If you have to reveal more cards than are left in your deck, first shuffle your discard pile and put it under your deck, then reveal the cards. If there still are not enough cards to reveal, you just reveal as many as you can.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
To **discard** a card is to move it into your **discard pile**. This is done every turn during your Clean-up phase, but can also be done at other times as part of the effect of a card. Cards that you play that cause you to discard from your hand are often sifters, or give you some benefit in exchange for discarding, while cards that cause other players to discard from their hand are handsize attacks. If you have a card on your Exile mat, you may discard it whenever you gain another copy of the same card.

There are several cards that do something when it or another card is discarded. See when-discard for a list of such cards and their effects.

Discarding is not to be confused with gaining a card (whether by buying it or otherwise) and putting it in your discard pile: this does not count as "discarding" the card. Further, Deck discarders (such as {card:Scavenger}), {card:Possession}, and {card:Order of Masons} also have effects that can move cards to a discard pile without officially "discarding" them.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
: "Discard a card" - Move a card from your hand to your discard pile.
* Sometimes a card will tell you to discard a card from another location, but by default discarded cards come from hands.
* You place the discarded card on top of your discard pile, face up.
* If you discard multiple cards at once, you do not need to allow others to see all of them, just the one you put on top.
* You can count the number of cards in your deck at any time (without looking at the card fronts), but cannot look through or count your discard pile or another player's deck or discard pile.
* When interacting with a discard pile (e.g. with {card:Harbinger}), it is not necessary to keep it in the same order. The only thing that ever matters about that order is that the top card is public.

See also When Discarded rules.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: **Gaining** a card adds it to the ones you own, usually by moving it to your discard pile.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
: "Gain a card" - Take a card from the Supply and put it into your discard pile.
* Sometimes a card will let you gain a card from a place other than the Supply, but by default gained cards come from the Supply.
* Sometimes a card will let you gain a card to a location other than your discard pile, but by default all gained cards are put into your discard pile.
* You do not play a card when you gain it; it just goes to your discard pile.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* If a card lets you gain a card to a location other than your discard pile, the gained card is put into that location no matter where it would normally go when gained. For example, {card:Artisan} lets you gain a {card:Nomad Camp} to your hand, even though Nomad Camp is usually gained onto your deck.
* If you are instructed to gain multiple cards, such as with {card:Develop} or {card:Prosper}, the cards are gained one at a time with any when-gain abilities being resolved before gaining the next card.

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: Gaining a card is a specific keyword in Dominion. By default, gained cards go onto your discard pile and come from the Supply. The most common way to gain cards is by Buying them; they are gained after being bought. Other ways mainly include through gainer cards. Some cards have abilities that trigger when the card is gained (e.g. {card:Border Village}) or when another card is gained (e.g. {card:Duplicate}).

sections.heading: Ownership
sections.body:
Gaining is not the only way to make a card yours. Any effect that moves a card to a location that is yours makes the card yours as well. You can take ownership of cards without gaining by:
* Being passed them (via {card:Masquerade})
* Exchanging something for them (e.g. {card:Changeling}, {card:Peasant}, {card:Trader})
* Exiling a card you don't own ({card:Camel Train}, {card:Coven}, {card:Invest}, and {card:Transport})
* Setting aside a card you don't own (e.g. {card:Inheritance})
* Trashing a card from the Supply which moves itself when trashed (e.g. using {card:Lurker} to trash a {card:Fortress}).
** Trashing these cards after they already belong to you also causes them to leave your ownership temporarily, and then return to it without being gained.

Abilities that trigger when a card is gained (or would be) won't trigger in these cases.

Buying a card also causes it to become yours at the moment it is bought (even before it is gained). This mattered before the 2022 Errata removed "when you buy" triggers. You lose ownership if another ability prevents the card from being gained (such as with {card:Possession} or older versions of {card:Trader}).

sections.heading: Gain location
Gaining from
sections.body: By default gained cards come from the Supply. You can't gain a card from somewhere else, such as the trash or a Non-Supply pile, unless explicitly instructed either to gain from that location, or to gain a non-Supply card by name. In the absence of an instruction to gain a *specific, named* Non-Supply card, or a card from a specific location, all gains come from the Supply; being instructed to gain "a copy of" a card not named specifically does not count as an exception.

sections.heading: Gain from trash
sections.body: See Trash gainer for a list of cards that can gain trashed cards.

sections.heading: Gain from non-Supply pile
Other
sections.body: {card:Black Market} allows you to buy from, and thereby gain from, a specially-constructed Black Market deck.

sections.heading: Who gains
When-gain
sections.body: Many cards do something when they are gained or when another card is gained. See when-gain for a list of such cards and how to resolve their effects.

sections.heading: Previous gains
sections.body:
Several cards care about previously gained cards.

* {card:Baths} — At the end of your turn, if you didn't gain any cards during your turn, take {vp:2} from Baths.
* {card:Commerce} — Gain a {card:Gold} per differently named card already gained this turn.
* {card:Conquest} — {vp:+1} per {card:Silver} gained this turn.
* {card:Destrier} — Costs {cost:1} less per card you've previously gained this turn.
* {card:Devil's Workshop} — If the number of cards gained this turn is 0 gain a Gold, if 1 gain a card costing up to {cost:4}, or otherwise gain an {card:Imp}.
* {card:Kintsugi} — Gains a card if you have gained a Gold during the game.
* {card:Monastery} — For each card gained this turn, you may trash a card from your hand or a {card:Copper} you have in play.
* {card:Merchant Guild} — At the end of your Buy phase, +1 Coffers per card you gained in it.
* {card:Receive Tribute} — If you've gained at least 3 cards this turn, gain up to 3 differently named Action cards you don't have copies of in play.
* {card:Smugglers} — Gain a copy of a card costing up to {cost:6} that the previous player gained on their last turn.
* {card:Treasure Hunter} — Gain a Silver per card the previous player gained in their last turn.
* {card:Triumph} — {vp:+1} per card gained this turn.
* {card:Wayfarer} — Has the same cost as the last other card gained this turn.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
To **set aside** a card is to place it on the table apart from your play area; such cards are not discarded during Clean-up, and are not considered to be "in play" for any purpose. This can be temporary, or permanent; in either case, if the game ends while you have cards set aside, they are returned to your deck before scores are calculated. Setting aside can be used as a way to mark cards as not required for the effect of an Action or Treasure being resolved, as a way to save cards for later use, or as a way to permanently remove a card from your deck without trashing it. Duration cards that are not discarded during Clean-up are not considered set aside; they are still in play.

Putting cards on mats is not technically setting them aside, but is equivivalent for most purposes (with exception of the Trash mat). See {card:Island}, {card:Native Village}, Reserve, and Exile.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
: "Set aside a card" - Put the card on the table, outside of the play area.
* Set aside cards are not "in play."
* Set aside cards are face up unless otherwise specified.
* A card that sets a card aside will say when to move it somewhere else.
