sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: **Adventures tokens** are those that come with the Adventures expansion. There are 10 different kinds, each in 6 colors (one for each player).

sections.heading: List of cards and Events that use tokens
sections.body: * Vanilla bonus tokens: — —

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
* Adventures has 10 tokens in each of 6 player colors.
* These are used with some Kingdom cards and Events.
* Tokens are counter-limited; there is just one of each per player, and players can never have more.

* Some tokens go on Action Supply piles.
* When gaining a card from a pile with a token on it, just tilt the card being taken to slide the tokens back onto the pile.
* The tokens still function on empty piles, and may be placed on empty piles. You can track what the empty pile was with its randomizer card turned sideways.
* Multiple tokens may be on the same pile; for example the green player might have a +1 Action and +1 Card token on a pile, while the blue player had a +1 Action token on the same pile.
* When multiple tokens are on a pile, they all function; the green player in that example would get both +1 Action and +1 Card when playing a card from that pile, in addition to the card's normal effects.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* If there is more than one differently named card in a pile, tokens on that pile still affect all cards in it.
* Many of the methods of placing these tokens specify placing them on Action Supply piles. Whether a pile is an "Action Supply pile" depends on the types listed on its randomizer.
** For example, the {card:Castles} pile contains Action cards but is not considered an Action supply pile; Odysseys and {card:Catapult/Rocks} are Action Supply piles even though not all cards in the pile are Actions.
** {card:Inheritance} and {card:Enlightenment} add the Action type to cards, but not the piles.
** However, {card:Seaway} and {card:Inheritance} do *not* care about the type of the pile when placing the token.

sections.heading: Preparation
sections.body: * If any tokens are being used, get them out of the box and keep them handy.

sections.heading: Vanilla bonus tokens
sections.body:
* Four tokens give +1 of something: +1 Action, +1 Buy, +1 Card, {coin:+1}.
* These tokens go on Action Supply piles.
* When the player whose token it is plays a card from that pile, that player first gets the bonus.
** For example a player with their +1 Action token on the {card:Ranger} pile will get +1 Action every time they play a Ranger.
* These tokens are used by {card:Teacher} and four Events: {card:Lost Arts} (+1 Action), {card:Seaway} (+1 Buy), {card:Pathfinding} (+1 Card), and {card:Training} ({coin:+1}).

**Other rules clarifications**
:* Drawing a card due to the +1 Card token happens before anything else that that card does; for example, if you play an Attack with the +1 Card token on its pile while {card:Urchin} (from Dark Ages) is in play, you draw a card before trashing Urchin and gaining a {card:Mercenary}.

sections.heading: –2 cost token
sections.body:
* The –{cost:2} cost token also goes on an Action Supply pile.
* It reduces the cost of cards from that pile on a particular player's turn.
* The –{cost:2} cost token lowers costs for all purposes; for example with a –{cost:2} cost token on {card:Gear}, a player could {card:Transmogrify} {card:Copper} into Gear.
* The –{cost:2} cost token does not lower costs below {cost:0}.
* This token is placed with {card:Ferry}.

sections.heading: Trashing token
sections.body:
* The Trashing token () also goes on an Action Supply pile.
* This token lets a player trash a card from their hand when gaining a card from that pile.
* This token is placed with {card:Plan}.

sections.heading: –1 Card token
sections.body:
* The large –1 Card token is placed onto a player's deck by {card:Relic}, {card:Borrow}, or {card:Raid}.
* It causes the player to draw one less card the next time they draw cards, and remove the token.
* This will reduce a regular draw of a new hand of 5 cards to 4 cards, or reduce the drawing from playing Actions or other effects.
* The token only has that effect once; then it is removed, and the player draws normally until the next time they have the token on their deck.
* The token only applies to draws; it does not affect revealing cards, nor does revealing cards remove the token (reveal the cards, then replace the token).
* The token applies to every card that says "+Cards" or "draw" and to no other cards; except, the promotional card Envoy says "{card:Envoy|draw the rest}" when it should say "{card:Envoy|put the rest into your hand};" it is not affected by the token.
* The token can go on an empty deck; it still applies.
* There is only one token per player; a player who already has the token on their deck is not further affected by being instructed to put the token there.
* Cards that draw up to a number of cards, such as {card:Watchtower} from Prosperity, skip a draw, removing the token, and then keep going, so that the token essentially did nothing.

**Other rules clarifications**
:* If your deck and discard pile are empty and you are instructed to draw a card, you will still remove this.
:* If you have no cards in your deck and you are instructed to draw one card, you remove this and you don't shuffle.
:* If you draw 0 cards (e.g. you play {card:Watchtower} with 8 cards in hand), you don't remove this.

sections.heading: –1 Coin token
sections.body:
* The large –{cost:1} token is placed in front of a player by {card:Bridge Troll} and {card:Ball}.
* It causes the player to get {cost:1} less the next time they get {cost:}; for example if the next {cost:} the player gets is from playing a {card:Gold}, instead of {cost:3} they would have {cost:2}.
* It is not removed by getting {coin:+0}, such as by playing {card:Miser} and choosing {coin:+} but having no {card:Copper|Coppers} on the Tavern mat.
* It applies to any source of {cost:}, such as Treasures, Action effects, and other effects like {card:Borrow}.
* It only applies once and then is removed, until the next time the player is given the token.
* There is only one token per player; a player who already has the token is not further affected by being instructed to take the token.

sections.heading: Journey token
sections.body:
* The Journey token () is face up at the start of a game.
* It can be turned over by {card:Ranger}, {card:Giant}, and {card:Pilgrimage}.
* They turn over the token and then check to see if it is face up or not, and do something based on that.
* The token can be turned face down with one effect and then face up with another.

**Other rules clarifications**
:* You don't flip this token like a coin; you just deliberately turn it over. It tracks that you get an effect every other play; it doesn't randomize when you get the effect.

sections.heading: Estate token
sections.body:
* The Estate token () is used by {card:Inheritance} to mark the card that a player's Estates have turned into.
* Once Inheritance is used, the token sits on a card near a player's play area (but not in play).

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
To **exchange** a card is to return it to its pile (Supply or otherwise) and put another card in the discard pile in its place. The card returned is not considered trashed, and the card received is not considered gained. Most cards that exchange themselves are in the two Traveller sequences in Adventures: chains of cards of increasing cost and power, where each one may be exchanged for the next stronger one when discarded from play (though the top two cards in these chains, {card:Champion} and {card:Teacher}, are not Travellers themselves).

Aside from Travellers:
* {card:Changeling} can be exchanged into when gaining another card,
* {card:Vampire} and {card:Bat} exchange into each other,
* {card:Trader} allows you to exchange any card you gain for {card:Silver},
* {card:Hermit} can be exchanged for a {card:Madman}.

sections.heading: From Adventures
sections.body:
* When a player discards a Traveller from play, they may exchange it for the card indicated; they return the card being exchanged to its pile, take the card they are exchanging it for, and puts that card into their discard pile.
* For example when exchanging {card:Peasant} for {card:Soldier}, they put Peasant back into its pile and takes a Soldier and puts it into their discard pile.
* Exchanging is not trashing or gaining, and so does not trigger abilities like {card:Travelling Fair|Travelling Fair's}.
* It is optional.
* It only happens when the card is discarded from play; discarding it from hand, such as due to not playing it, will not trigger it.
* It only happens if the card being exchanged for has any copies available; if there are no Soldiers in the pile, Peasant cannot be exchanged at that time.
* If multiple cards do something when discarded from play, the player picks the order; for example, with no Soldiers left in the pile, a player with Peasant and Soldier in play could first exchange Soldier for {card:Fugitive}, then exchange Peasant for that Soldier.

sections.heading: From Nocturne
sections.body: * Nocturne has three cards that tell a player to "exchange" a card for another card. The card being exchanged is returned to its Supply pile, or non-Supply pile, and the card being exchanged for is taken and put into the player's discard pile. This does not count as gaining a card. The exchange only happens if both cards can be exchanged; if the pile is empty, the cards are not exchanged.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* Unlike gaining, exchanging can happen with a non-Supply pile without special instructions. For instance, you can use {card:Trader} to exchange a {card:Horse} for a {card:Silver} even though the Horse pile is not part of the Supply.
* The card being returned as part of the exchange must have a pile to go back to. Therefore cards that don't have piles of their own anywhere, such as Shelters, Heirlooms, or Zombies, or cards whose piles have been removed by {card:Divine Wind}, cannot be involved in an exchange.
* The {card:Black Market} deck is not considered a pile; so for example if a Traveller, {card:Vampire}, or {card:Hermit} is bought using {card:Black Market}, there is no pile to return it to and therefore it cannot be exchanged.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
A small number of cards tell the player to spend an amount of coins ({cost:}) already produced, in order to get a certain bonus out of them other than their normal use in buying things, and usually outside the Buy phase, when coins are typically spent. Cards having a pay effect are:
* {card:Asceticism} — provides trashing.
* {card:Capital City} — gives an optional extra draw effect
* {card:Pageant} — lets the player convert {cost:} produced in a turn into saveable Coffers
* {card:Storyteller} — provides a draw effect

Debt is also removed by paying it off; and overpaying allows you to spend additional {cost:} when buying a card for a bonus effect.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:

**Debt** (represented by the symbol {debt:}) is an alternate cost for some cards and Events in Empires and Rising Sun. It allows the buyer to take {debt:} tokens rather than paying {cost:} immediately to buy the card. Players who have {debt:} tokens may not buy cards, Events, or Projects. {debt:} tokens can be removed from a player by paying {cost:1} per {debt:} token at any time during their turn.

A cost in {debt:} is orthogonal to a cost in a {cost:}; cards with {debt:} in their cost do not cost less or more than cards with a {cost:} cost. {debt:} and {potion} are similarly not comparable.

Apart from buying things with a {debt:} cost, {debt:} tokens can be accumulated in a handful of other ways, mainly as as a result of playing certain cards.

Empires and Rising Sun both come with 40 {card:Debt tokens}, but the mechanic is not intended to be component-limited.

sections.heading: Debt as a cost
Other sources of Debt
sections.body:
* {card:Change}, {card:Craftsman}, {card:Gold Mine}, {card:Imperial Envoy}, {card:Litter}, and {card:Root Cellar} can give {debt:} when you play them.
* {card:Capital} gives you {debt:} when it is discarded from play during the Clean-up phase.
* {card:Credit} allows you to gain a card and take {debt:} corresponding to its cost in {cost:}.
* {card:Tax} and {card:Harsh Winter} put {debt:} on card piles, and make you take the {debt:} when you gain cards from such a pile.
* {card:Mountain Pass} is a Landmark where players bid {debt:} for 8{vp:}, taking the {debt:} they bid if they win.

sections.heading: Official rules
sections.body:
<onlyinclude>
* Having {card:Debt tokens} prevents a player from buying cards or Events; Debt tokens do nothing else (for example they have no effect at the end of the game).
* Buying a card or Event with {debt:} in its cost gives the player that many Debt tokens.
* A player can remove Debt tokens <abbr title="This is an amended rule from August 2024.">at any point in their turn</abbr> by paying {cost:1} per Debt token to remove it.
* Removing Debt does not use up a Buy [or an Action, and can be done multiple times in a turn. This does not let players play Treasures at any time.]

* {debt:} amounts are something different from {cost:}.  Math involving {cost:} amounts does not affect {debt:} amounts.
* [Some cards look for a cost in a range.]
** *Empires:*  {debt:4} is not "up to {cost:4}."  {debt:4} is not more than {cost:4}  and {cost:4} is not more than {debt:4};  both have something the other lacks.
**
*Rising Sun:*  "Up to {cost:4}" means "{cost:0}, {cost:1}, {cost:2}, {cost:3}, or {cost:4}";  it does not include costs with {debt:} in them.

* [Some cards compare costs.]
** *Empires:*  An amount of {cost:} and {debt:} is only larger than another if both the {cost:} and {debt:} amounts are larger, or one is larger and one the same. Amounts that do not specify {cost:} have {cost:0}, and amounts that do not specify {debt:} have {debt:0} (including all previous Dominion card costs).
**
*Rising Sun:*  A card costing {debt:8} costs more than one costing {debt:6}, just like one costing {cost:8} costs more than one costing {cost:6}.  However debt and {cost:} are not comparable. With a card costing {cost:4} and a card costing {debt:6}, neither costs more than the other.  {debt:6} does however cost more than {cost:0}; there is an implicit {cost:0} in all pure {debt:} costs, so {debt:6} costs the same amount of {cost:} as {cost:0}, and more {debt:}.

* Players cannot just take Debt tokens for no reason.
* Players cannot overpay with Debt (for Dominion: Guilds cards).
* Debt tokens are not counter-limited; players should use a replacement if they run out.</onlyinclude>
*
{card:Possession} (from Dominion: Alchemy) now has errata that causes it to also give the Possessing player all Debt tokens the Possessed player would get.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.body:
* *Empires:*  Natalie has {cost:4} and buys {card:City Quarter}, which costs {debt:8}.  She takes {debt:8}, then immediately pays off {debt:4} with her {cost:4}.  She still has {debt:4}.  On her next turn, in her Buy phase, she has {cost:3}.  She cannot buy any cards; all she can do is pay off {debt:3}, leaving her with {debt:1}.  On her next turn, in her Buy phase, she has {cost:6}.  She pays off the {debt:1} and has {cost:5} left to spend.  She buys an {card:Engineer}, taking {debt:4} and immediately paying {cost:4} to get rid of it.

* *Rising Sun:*  Kate has {cost:4} and buys {card:Daimyo}, which costs {debt:6}.  She takes {debt:6}, then immediately pays off {debt:4} with her {cost:4}.  She still has {debt:2}.  On her next turn, in her Buy phase, she has {cost:5}.  She pays off the remaining {debt:2} and has {cost:3} left, with which she buys a {card:Silver}.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.body:
* *Empires:*  {card:Patrician} checks to see if a card costs "{cost:5} or more."  {card:Fortune} costs {cost:8}{debt:8}, so it costs "{cost:5} or more."  {card:Overlord} costs {debt:8};  that is not "{cost:5} or more."
* *Rising Sun:*  {card:Craftsman} can't gain a {card:Mountain Shrine}, because {debt:5} is not "up to {cost:5}."  {card:Poet} cannot draw a {card:Mountain Shrine}, because {debt:5} is not "up to {cost:3}.

* *Empires:*  {card:Bridge} (from Dominion: Intrigue) lowers the cost of cards by {cost:1}.  This lowers Fortune from {cost:8}{debt:8} to {cost:7}{debt:8},  but has no effect on {card:Engineer|Engineer's} cost of {debt:4}.
* *Rising Sun:*  {card:Flourishing Trade} lowers costs, but has no effect on the cost of {card:Daimyo}.

* *Empires:*  {card:Knights} (from Dominion: Dark Ages) trash cards costing from {cost:3} to {cost:6}. That never includes cards with {debt:} in the cost.
* *Rising Sun:*  {card:Change} can't gain a {card:Mountain Shrine}, no matter what you trash, because Mountain Shrine doesn't cost any {cost:}.

* *Empires:*  {card:Trader} (from Dominion: Hinterlands) trashes a card and gives a {card:Silver} per {cost:1} it cost. {card:Trader} trashing {card:Fortune} would give 8 Silvers for the {cost:8}, and no additional Silvers for the {debt:8}.
* *Rising Sun:*  {card:Tanuki} trashing an {card:Artist} can gain a {card:Daimyo}, because Daimyo does cost "up to {cost:2} and {debt:8}."

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: **Exile** is a place to put cards that was introduced in Menagerie. If there are any cards in the Kingdom that use Exile, give an **Exile mat** to each player. When you Exile a card, you put it on your Exile mat. Exiling a card is not gaining it or trashing it. Cards on your Exile mat are yours, regardless of whether the card was yours before it was put there (e.g. Exiling a card from the Supply makes that card yours). When you gain a card, you may discard all the other copies of it you have in Exile. You cannot discard only some of the copies; you must either discard all of them, or none of them.

sections.heading: Exile
sections.body:
Menagerie has Exile mats that cards can go on. Each player gets one.
* "Exile a card" means, put it on your Exile mat.
* "Cards in Exile" are the cards on your mat.
* Cards on your mat are yours; at the end of the game, include them when scoring.
* The cards on Exile mats are face up and public.
* When you gain a card, you may discard the other copies of it from your mat.
** For example, if you have two {card:Silver|Silvers} on your mat, and gain a Silver, you may discard the two Silvers from your mat - they go to your discard pile. You can leave them on the mat instead. You cannot discard just one of them.
* Exiling a card from the Supply is not "gaining" the card, and will not cause "when you gain this" abilities to happen.
* Discarding a card from your Exile mat is not gaining it either.
* Discarding a card from your Exile mat is discarding a card; if it happens other than in Clean-up, it can trigger {card:Tunnel} (from Hinterlands) or {card:Village Green}.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
To **rotate** a pile with differently-named cards in it is to move all copies of one card on top of the pile to the bottom, so as to expose the next differently-named card in the pile.

This mechanic was introduced in Allies, in which there are split piles containing four copies each of four differently-named cards. The cheapest card in each pile allows you to rotate the pile, enabling you to reach the more expensive cards below without having to gain all copies of the cheap cards first, or to hide a desirable card from your opponent by rotating it to the bottom before they can gain one.

sections.heading: Official rules (from Allies)
sections.body:
* The top card of each split pile has an ability that can "rotate" the pile (or with {card:Battle Plan}, any pile).
* Rotating a pile means taking the top card, and all copies of it directly under it, and putting them on the bottom.
** For example, if three {card:Herb Gatherer|Herb Gatherers} were at the top of the {card:Augurs}, followed by {card:Acolyte|Acolytes}, you would put those three Herb Gatherers on the bottom, and Acolyte would now be on top.

sections.heading: Other rules clarifications
sections.body:
* {card:Battle Plan} can rotate any Supply pile, not just the split piles from Allies. This includes {card:Knights} and Ruins from Dark Ages and other split piles (for example {card:Castles} and {card:Sauna/Avanto}).
* If a split pile is chosen as the pile for {card:Ferryman}, the pile can still be rotated by cards that refer to the pile by its name even though the pile is not in the Supply.
* As Battle Plan can only rotate Supply piles, it cannot rotate the Ferryman's pile, even if that pile is {card:Clashes}.
* When cards are returned to their piles out of order via an effect such as {card:Swap} or {card:Way of the Horse}, rotating only affects consecutive cards of the same name on top of the pile. For instance, if the {card:Wizards} pile has a {card:Student} on top of four {card:Lich}es and then two more Students below that, rotating the pile will only move the top Student and leave the rest of the Students where they are.

* {card:Student} — Rotates the {card:Wizards} pile.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: To **return** a card is to put it back onto its pile (Supply or otherwise).

sections.heading: Rules
sections.body:
* The returned card is placed on the top of the pile.
* If the pile is a split pile, the card is returned on the top even if a different card is currently on top, covering it.
* The card returned is not considered trashed.
* Non-Supply cards, for example Rewards or {card:Spoils}, can be returned.
** Originally, the cards were phrased to only allow returning cards to the Supply, however with the 2022 Errata this changed to allow cards to be returned to any pile. As *{card:Ambassador}* was removed it has not been updated and still only allows returning cards to Supply piles.
* Only cards that belong to a pile can be returned. Notably, the {card:Black Market} deck is not considered a pile meaning cards from it cannot be returned.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Several cards instructs you to **name a card**, often followed by revealing cards from your deck and acting based on whether the revealed card(s) match the name. This often results in a gambling based on how well you know the content of your deck, but with the help of cards like {card:Secret Passage}, cards can be named with certainty.

sections.heading: Rules clarifications
sections.body:
* When naming a card, it must be a card's name to match. Saying a type, such as "Treasure", will not match any cards.
* Cards from split piles are different cards and must be matched specifically, e.g. naming "Ruins" or "Ruined Market" will not match {card:Ruined Village}.
* The name must be exact, e.g. naming "Village" will only match {card:Village}, not {card:Fishing Village}.
* A card's name is never changed, e.g. {card:Estate|Estates} under the influence of {card:Inheritance} do not match the name of the card they inherit.
* When naming a card, you can choose to say the wrong name even if you know what card is about to be revealed. You can name any card, even if you know that it cannot be in your deck.

* {card:Mystic} — Name a card and reveal one card, putting it into your hand if it is the named card.

**Victory tokens** (usually abbreviated as **VP tokens** or {vp:} tokens) can be gained by certain cards, Events, and Landmarks in Prosperity and Empires. They keep a tally of how much {vp:} a player has accrued over the game by means other than Victory cards. They are represented by metal shields similar to the icon used on Victory cards, in units of {vp:1}, {vp:2} and {vp:5}. Prosperity comes with 16 {vp:1} tokens and 15 {vp:5} tokens, while Empires comes with 24 {vp:1} tokens, 12 {vp:2} tokens and 20 {vp:5} tokens; if they run out, players can use another means to count their {vp:}.

* The {vp:} tokens are simply tokens that are worth {vp:} at the end of the game. They provide a way to score that is not cards in a player's deck.
* They come in {vp:1} and {vp:5} amounts; make change as needed. They are not counter-limited; use a replacement if you run out.
* Cards say "{vp:+1}" (or other amounts) to indicate that a player takes {vp:} tokens. Cards that give {vp:+} take the tokens from the pile of unused tokens, not from a player.

sections.heading: Randomizers
sections.body:
Randomizers are cards that can be used during the setup of a game to choose a random Kingdom. They have backs with blue borders to differentiate them from deck cards that have a tan border.

There are a few notable randomizers, such as for split piles, with important information on the front side.

sections.heading: Blank cards
sections.body:
Blank cards are provided for creating your own Kingdom card.

These can easily be re-used, by writing on sets of ten something like "A" or "B" and then having a reference nearby as you play to tell you what exactly "A" and "B" mean in this game.

As cards are printed in sets of 50, sets where the amount of cards doesn't add up to an even multiple of 50 have a few blank cards. When possible, the number of cards in a set is generally adjusted to use up all space so no blank cards are needed. This is notable from the sometimes odd number of Landscape cards in recent sets, the 5 Prizes in Cornucopia, and the 16 {card:Potion|Potions} in Alchemy.

Blank cards are available in the following sets:
* Base — 4 (was 7 before Second Edition)
* Intrigue — 6 (was 8 before Second Edition)
* Seaside — 1 (was 12 before Second Edition)
* Prosperity — 1
* Hinterlands — 10 (was 8 before Second Edition)
* Guilds (before combined with Cornucopia) — 7
* Guilds & Cornucopia before Second Edition — 6
* Adventures — 6

**Split piles** are Kingdom card piles containing multiple differently named cards, in a particular order. Often, the cards in a split pile have some particular synergy with each other. Split piles were introduced in Empires and revisited in Allies. In Empires, the cards on top of the pile had to be gained or trashed before the cards on the bottom would be available; but Allies introduced the mechanism of rotating a split pile, allowing the top cards to be moved to the bottom of the pile to make the next cards accessible.

Dark Ages featured Knights and Ruins, a precursor to split piles; these Supply piles contain multiple differently-named cards, but they are shuffled at the start of the game rather than appearing in a prescribed order.

The cards in a split pile usually have different costs and may belong to different card types. When an effect depends on the cost or types *of a pile*, rather than of an individual card, the information listed on a split pile's randomizer card determines what the cost and types of the pile as a whole are considered to be. For instance, the {card:Gladiator/Fortune} pile is labeled a {cost:3} Action pile, and therefore may be designated the Bane pile for {card:Young Witch} and have various Adventures tokens placed on it, even though {card:Fortune} is not an Action and costs more than {cost:3}; and when this is the case, Fortune and {card:Gladiator} both receive the bonuses from the Adventures tokens and may be used as a Bane card.

sections.heading: Empires
sections.body:
Five Kingdom Card piles in Empires have two cards in them, with 5 copies of each - {card:Catapult} / {card:Rocks}, {card:Encampment} / {card:Plunder}, {card:Gladiator} / {card:Fortune}, {card:Patrician} / {card:Emporium}, and {card:Settlers} / {card:Bustling Village}. The Randomizers for those piles show both cards.
* During set-up, always put the cheaper card on top, e.g. Patrician (cost {cost:2}) above Emporium (cost {cost:5}).
* To mark the pile, turn the bottom half sideways. That way players remember that the other card is there. Turn it back when those cards are uncovered.
* Players may only Buy or Gain the top card of a pile; players have to work through the top 5 cards to get to the bottom 5.
* Players can read the covered card to remember what it does, but cannot buy it or gain it until it is uncovered.
* If the card is covered back up somehow - for example Encampment can return to its pile - then once again players cannot Buy or Gain the covered cards, until again uncovered.
* Returning cards to a pile, such as with {card:Ambassador} (from Dominion: Seaside), can also result in the pile being in an unusual order; an Ambassador could return a Plunder to the Encampment/Plunder pile on top of an Encampment.
* Some cards refer to the cost or types of a pile as if it is just one card. In these cases go with what is on the Randomizer card, which usually matches the top card.
* Some things refer to cards from a particular pile; these things work on both cards from a split pile.
* For example {card:Training} (from Dominion: Adventures) lets a player put a token on an Action pile, which causes them to get {coin:+1} when playing a card from that pile. The token can be put on the Catapult / Rocks pile, despite Rocks being a Treasure; and the token causes both Catapult and Rocks to produce an extra {cost:1} when played.
* Emptying the top half of a split pile does not count as emptying a pile, for the game end condition or cards that refer to empty piles. The entire pile needs to be gone for the pile to be empty.
* One Kingdom Card pile in Empires has 8 different cards - the {card:Castles}. They behave similarly to the other split piles; only the top card can be bought or gained, they go in order by cost with {card:Humble Castle} on top, and so on. This pile is treated as a Victory - Castle pile, as per the Randomizer, despite the top card being a Treasure - Victory - Castle. In 2-player games, use one of each Castle; with more players, use all 12 cards.

sections.heading: Allies
sections.body:
Dominion: Allies has six split piles, that have four different cards in each of them.
* The cards start the game in order by cost. For example, the {card:Augurs} pile starts out with 4 {card:Herb Gatherer|Herb Gatherers} on top, then 4 {card:Acolyte|Acolytes}, then 4 {card:Sorceress|Sorceresses}, then 4 {card:Sibyl|Sibyls}. This order may get messed up by cards like {card:Swap}; that's fine.
* As with the split piles in Dominion: Empires, only the top card of a split pile can be bought or gained.
* You can look through the cards in a split pile at any time, without changing the order.
* The top card of each split pile has an ability that can "rotate" the pile (or with {card:Battle Plan}, any pile). Rotating a pile means taking the top card, and all copies of it directly under it, and putting them on the bottom. For example, if three Herb Gatherers were at the top of the Augurs, followed by Acolytes, you would put those three Herb Gatherers on the bottom, and Acolyte would now be on top.
* Some cards refer to information about a pile as if it's just one card. In these cases, go with what's on the Randomizer card, which usually matches the top card.
* Some things refer to cards from a particular pile; these things work on all cards from a split pile. For example {card:Training} (from Dominion: Adventures) lets a player put a token on an Action pile, which causes them to get {coin:+1} when playing a card from that pile. The token can be put on the {card:Odysseys|Odyssey} pile, and then {card:Sunken Treasure} will also make {coin:+1} when played.

Several cards that were published in the first editions of the earliest sets in Dominion were **removed** from those sets, and replaced by new cards, when their second editions were released. Cards chosen for removal were chiefly those that turned out to be underpowered or rarely useful in gameplay, as well as a few overpowered cards that tended to dominate games they were in.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.body: Overall, most people were content with the early upgrades, praising the removal of weak cards and the addition of a handful of exciting new cards. The only controversy among the revisions to the base set and Intrigue came from the removal of {card:Coppersmith} from the second edition of Intrigue, which many frequent forum members were unhappy about. Coppersmith, while not a power card, was probably the strongest of the removed cards, and a fairly unique one as well. It was argued that Coppersmith was mainly removed because it tends to be a trap card for newer players; while occasionally useful as payload in an engine, it is typically a card newer players buy early on in the game, only to regret it a few turns later. A poll on the Dominion Strategy forums revealed that a little under 40% of forum members would miss Coppersmith the most out of the removed cards.

Overview
sections.body:
The **second edition** of Dominion consists of large updates to several early sets. It mainly involved the removal of some cards that, in retrospect, seemed weak or not fun to play with and replacing them with new cards.

The second editions of the - Dominion set and - coincided with the 2016 Errata, and incorporate all those changes in addition to the changes described on this page.

The second editions of -, -, and - coincided with the 2022 Errata and incorporate those and earlier changes.

The second edition of - was released in 2024.

sections.heading: Changes
sections.body:
The biggest changes are the removal of several cards in each set and new cards added in their place. Some new cards are direct replacements (such as {card:Patrol} for {card:Scout}), but others filled needs that Donald X. had felt were lacking in the sets. For instance, the first edition of the base set had several big money enablers, but not a lot of engine support, leading some players of the base game to view it as a solved game where you could win by mostly buying Treasures, so the second edition added several cantrips to balance the set strategically.

The new cards added to each set are available separately as Update Packs, allowing owners of the first-edition sets to get the new cards without buying the entire set again.

All second-edition sets have new box cover art and icons that makes it easy to distinguish them from the first-edition boxes and cards.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
**Card-shaped thing** is an informal term encompassing Dominion cards as well as gameplay components that are printed on physical cards but not considered "cards" by the game rules. To distinguish these other components from cards, they are printed in landscape orientation and are sometimes referred to as **landscapes**, **sideways cards**, or **horizontals**.

For a full list of all card components, see List of cards and Special cards.

For a summary of the number of cards in each expansion and information related to storing and sleeving cards, see Card storage.

sections.heading: Cards
sections.body:
Any reference within the game to "card" or "cards" refer to any of these cards.
* Basic cards — These are the piles that are used in every game, like {card:Silver} and {card:Province}, but also the additional basic cards added by expansions such as {card:Colony} and Ruins.
* Kingdom cards — These are the cards from which the Kingdom (normally 10 piles) are chosen for each game.
* Non-Supply cards — These are other cards that are used actively during the game (i.e. they can be part of players' decks) but they are not part of the Supply and must therefore be gained in other ways.

Cards have one or more types, the most basic being Action, Treasure, and Victory. See card types for a list of each type and its purpose.

sections.heading: Special cards
sections.body:
These cards are not used actively during gameplay.
* Randomizers — Cards with blue backs that can be used to randomly chose the Kingdom piles.
* Blank cards — Spare cards with the standard back but no content on the front. Can be used as replacements for lost cards or to make your own cards.
* The Trash pile card — Used to mark the trash pile in the first edition of Dominion and Intrigue. Was replaced by a mat in the second edition.

sections.heading: Landscape orientation
sections.body:
Certain landscape types function similarly to Kingdom cards in terms of selection for inclusion in a game, in that they may be included or excluded from a given game of Dominion regardless of what Kingdom cards or other landscapes are present. One possible method of choosing is to shuffle these card-shaped things into the randomizer cards, and use whichever landscapes are dealt out while dealing out ten Kingdom cards. It is generally recommended that no more than two in total out of any of the following types be used in a game:
* Events
* Landmarks
* Projects
* Ways
* Traits

Other landscapes' presence in games depends on whether certain Kingdom cards, or types of Kingdom cards, are present:

* Boons: in a game with Fate cards, all 12 Boons are generally used.
* Hexes: in a game with Doom cards, all 12 Hexes are used.
* States: the state {card:Lost in the Woods} is used with the Kingdom card {card:Fool}; other States are used with Doom cards.
* Artifacts: each of the five Artifacts is used with a specific Kingdom card.
* Allies: in a game with Liaison cards, one Ally is selected at the start of the game.
* Prophecies: in a game with Omen cards, one Prophecy is selected at the start of the game.
